title: Anterior compartment syndrome: deep peroneal nerve
vignette: A 29-year-old previously healthy man comes to the hospital with a right leg injury after a cycling accident. He reports pain in the lower leg and inability to bear weight. X-ray reveals right tibial and fibular shaft fractures. The patient undergoes closed reduction and immobilization of the fractures. Several hours later, he has increasingly severe pain in his right leg. Physical examination shows increased tension within the anterior compartment. Of the leg's four fascial compartments, the anterior compartment contains the foot/toe extensor muscles, the anterior tibial artery, and the deep peroneal (fibular) nerve. Which of the following structures is most likely to be compromised by this patient's acute complication?

clues.text: right tibial and fibular shaft fractures
clues.note: Long-bone (tibial) fractures are the most common cause of acute compartment syndrome - bleeding/edema raises pressure within the inelastic fascial compartment.

clues.text: increasingly severe pain in his right leg
clues.note: Pain out of proportion (and worsening after immobilization) is the earliest sign of acute compartment syndrome, which threatens the contents of the compartment.

clues.text: increased tension within the anterior compartment
clues.note: A tense ANTERIOR compartment localizes the syndrome. The anterior compartment of the leg contains the deep peroneal (fibular) nerve, so that nerve is at risk.

whatMatters: A tibial fracture with worsening pain and a tense ANTERIOR compartment = acute compartment syndrome of the leg's anterior compartment - the most common site. The anterior compartment contains the foot extensors, anterior tibial artery, and the DEEP PERONEAL (fibular) NERVE, which is compromised (weak dorsiflexion/foot drop, decreased sensation in the first web space). Answer A.
strategy: Localize to the ANTERIOR compartment, then recall its neurovascular contents: deep peroneal nerve + anterior tibial artery + toe/foot extensors. The nerve at risk is the DEEP peroneal nerve (A). Reject structures in OTHER compartments: great saphenous vein (superficial, outside fascia), peroneal veins/tibial nerve/posterior tibial artery (posterior compartments), superficial peroneal nerve (lateral compartment).

eliminations.label: Great saphenous vein - superficial, outside fascia
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the great (long) saphenous vein runs superficially along the medial leg, outside the deep fascia. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it isn't within a fascial compartment, so it is not compressed by compartment syndrome. ✅ Correct if: asking about a superficial venous structure (e.g., for grafting).

eliminations.label: Peroneal veins - lateral/posterior drainage
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the peroneal veins accompany the peroneal artery draining the lateral/posterior leg. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: they aren't in the anterior compartment. ✅ Correct if: a lateral/posterior compartment question.

eliminations.label: Posterior tibial artery - deep posterior compartment
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the posterior tibial artery lies in the deep posterior compartment. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: wrong compartment - it's not compromised by an ANTERIOR compartment syndrome. ✅ Correct if: deep posterior compartment syndrome (plantar sensory loss, toe flexion weakness).

eliminations.label: Superficial peroneal nerve - lateral compartment
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the superficial peroneal nerve runs in the LATERAL compartment (with the peroneus muscles). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it's in a different compartment; lateral compartment syndrome gives dorsolateral foot sensory loss and eversion weakness. ✅ Correct if: lateral compartment syndrome.

eliminations.label: Tibial nerve - posterior compartment
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the tibial nerve travels in the deep posterior compartment. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: wrong compartment for this anterior syndrome. ✅ Correct if: deep posterior compartment syndrome.

reasoning: Tibial fracture is the most common cause of acute compartment syndrome
Worsening pain + a tense compartment after immobilization = acute compartment syndrome
The affected ANTERIOR compartment contains the deep peroneal nerve (plus anterior tibial artery and toe extensors)
-> deep peroneal nerve is compromised; answer A
mechanism: The leg is divided by inelastic deep fascia and the interosseous membrane into four compartments (anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, deep posterior). When pressure inside a compartment rises - most commonly from long-bone (tibial) fracture with hemorrhage/edema - perfusion falls, producing acute compartment syndrome with pain out of proportion, and later paresthesia, pallor, pulselessness, and paralysis; urgent fasciotomy is needed to prevent myonecrosis, nerve injury, and amputation. The ANTERIOR compartment (the most common site) contains the foot/toe extensor muscles, the anterior tibial artery, and the DEEP PERONEAL (fibular) NERVE; its compression causes weak dorsiflexion (foot drop) and decreased sensation in the first web space between the great and second toes. The distractor structures lie outside this compartment: the great saphenous vein is superficial; the peroneal veins, tibial nerve, and posterior tibial artery are in the lateral/posterior compartments; and the superficial peroneal nerve is in the lateral compartment.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Anatomy > leg compartments: anterior = deep peroneal nerve + anterior tibial artery + foot extensors (foot drop, first web-space sensory loss); acute compartment syndrome after tibial fracture.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Localize to the anterior compartment, then recall which nerve/artery it contains (deep peroneal nerve).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on compartment syndrome, deep vs superficial peroneal nerve, dorsiflexion, or fasciotomy? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Superficial peroneal nerve (lateral compartment) and tibial nerve/posterior tibial artery (posterior) are the wrong-compartment traps; the great saphenous vein is superficial (outside fascia).

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.message: On the leg cross-section, find the anterior compartment (front, next to the tibia) - it holds the deep peroneal nerve and anterior tibial artery. Anchor: 'front of the leg = deep peroneal nerve.'

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: anterior compartment syndrome (most common; tibial fracture) -> deep peroneal nerve -> foot drop + first web-space numbness; fasciotomy.
